elements.quote: In addition, we included a summary of findings table for the primary outcomes of this review (Table 2). It included the number of participants and studies for each outcome, a summary of the intervention effect, and a measure of the quality of evidence for each outcome according to GRADE considerations.
elements.reason: Methods describe the tables used (Table 1 characteristics of included studies, Table 2 summary of findings with GRADE) and their contents.

elements.quote: Forest plot was generated for each comparison.
elements.reason: Graphical displays are described: forest plots for each comparison and a risk of bias summary figure (Fig 2) mentioned in text_14.
No reported basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs is provided in the retrieved evidence.
Only standard displays (forest plots, risk of bias figure, standard tables) are reported; no non-standard graphs are described, so no rationale is required.

elements.quote: Meta-analysis was conducted using Review Manager (Revman) version 5.2.[29]
elements.reason: Software and version (RevMan 5.2) are explicitly reported.

elements.quote: In case of considerable heterogeneity (I 2 > 75%) we only carried out a narrative synthesis of the results and grouped our findings by the type of outcome measured.
elements.reason: Alternative narrative synthesis is described when meta-analysis was not appropriate.

elements.quote: We used the random-effects model for all analyses, to incorporate any existing heterogeneity.
elements.reason: Random-effects model reported with a rationale.

elements.quote: Meta-analyses of the correct effect estimates and standard errors from cRCTs were pooled using generic inverse-variance methods in RevMan 2012.
elements.reason: Statistical pooling method (generic inverse-variance; RR/MD effect measures) is reported.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity among the studies included in meta-analysis was assessed by visual inspection of overlap of confidence intervals, and by assessing statistical heterogeneity with the Chi 2 statistic (P < 0.1). I 2 statistic was computed to quantify heterogeneity; an I 2 of 75% and above was taken as an indicator of more than desired heterogeneity.
elements.reason: Heterogeneity assessment (Chi-squared, I-squared, visual inspection, thresholds) is fully described.
Random-effects model used, but the between-study variance estimator (e.g., DerSimonian-Laird, REML) is not reported.
95% CIs are reported, but the method used to calculate confidence intervals for the random-effects summary effect is not described.
No additional random-effects implementation details (e.g., tau-squared handling) are reported beyond the model choice.
Meta-analysis was frequentist using RevMan; no Bayesian methods were used.

elements.quote: For interventions with multiple comparison groups, all groups that met the inclusion criteria were included in the review and meta-analyses.[31] If there were more than two relevant comparison groups we combined the relevant experimental and control groups to generate a single pair wise comparison.
elements.reason: Handling of multiple estimates per study (group combination to create a single pairwise comparison) is described; design-effect adjustment for clustering is also reported.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity of costing methodologies, outcomes, preclude quantitative synthesis of economic estimates.
elements.reason: The impossibility of quantitative synthesis for economic data is stated, but reasons for other planned syntheses judged inappropriate are less systematically reported beyond the general I-squared >75% rule.

elements.quote: In order to compare the different subgroups with each other, we conducted a standard heterogeneity test across the subgroup results, by calculating the I-square statistic... In addition, we also performed a sensitivity analyses to assess the influence of study size and study design on the findings.
elements.reason: Methods to explore heterogeneity (I-square heterogeneity testing, subgroup analysis, sensitivity analyses) are explicitly described.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses was performed by... the age and sex of participants, and sensitivity analyses was conducted to assess the robustness of the findings.
elements.reason: Subgroup factors (age, sex) are named, but factor levels and expected direction of effect modification are not reported.
No statement about whether subgroup analyses used study-level variables or within-study contrasts.

elements.quote: we conducted a standard heterogeneity test across the subgroup results, by calculating the I-square statistic. During subgroup analysis, we ensured that the subgroup data being compared were independent.
elements.reason: An I-square test across subgroups and ensuring independence are reported, but no formal test for interaction/difference between subgroup effects is described.

elements.quote: In case of considerable heterogeneity (I 2 > 75%) we only carried out a narrative synthesis of the results and grouped our findings by the type of outcome measured.
elements.reason: Narrative synthesis when meta-analysis unsuitable is described with grouping by outcome type, but other factors and their levels for exploring heterogeneity informally are not detailed.
No identification of which heterogeneity analyses were not pre-specified; no distinction between pre-specified and post-hoc analyses is made.

elements.quote: In addition, we also performed a sensitivity analyses to assess the influence of study size and study design on the findings.
elements.reason: Methods describe sensitivity analyses assessing influence of study size and design; results (text_25, text_26, table_4) report leave-one-out sensitivity analyses with revised effect estimates for each outcome.
No evidence indicates whether sensitivity analyses were pre-specified or identifies any as not pre-specified.

elements.quote: Likelihood of reporting bias through funnel plots was assessed only for blood pressure outcomes. There was substantial evidence of funnel plot asymmetry for both SBP and DBP, suggesting evidence of small study bias (Fig 5).
elements.reason: Funnel plot assessment of reporting bias is reported, but only in the Results and limited to blood pressure outcomes; no formal methods description (e.g., test for asymmetry) is provided in the Methods.

elements.quote: Additionally, Cochrane risk of bias tool was used to assess risk of bias.[25] For each item, a judgement of 'High risk', 'Unclear risk', or 'Low risk' was made.
elements.reason: The Cochrane tool with selective reporting domain is used (Fig 2 risk of bias summary shows 'Selective reporting (reporting bias)'), but the process for deriving an overall judgement for reporting bias specifically is not described.
No adaptations to an existing reporting-bias tool are described.
No newly developed reporting-bias tool is reported.

elements.quote: Reviewers independently dual-rated study quality and applicability using established criteria. Discrepancies were resolved through a consensus process wherein all four reviewers jointly analysed and discussed each article.
elements.reason: Number of reviewers, independent dual rating, and consensus-based disagreement resolution are reported for quality/risk-of-bias rating.

elements.quote: minor queries related to data or outcome were there, for which we contacted the study's primary author via email. We recorded all missing secondary outcome data in the data extraction form and in the risk of bias table.
elements.reason: The process of contacting study investigators to confirm or obtain missing information is reported, though not specific to reporting bias.
No automation tools were used for reporting-bias assessment according to the evidence.

elements.quote: GRADEWorking Group grades of evidence: High quality: Further research is very unlikely to change our confidence in the estimate of effect.

elements.quote: A major limitation observed was the low magnitude of effect and quality of evidence in study trials included in this review. elements.quote: Interventions included community health worker led health education/health promotion (life style modification advice) for diabetes, cancer, cardiovascular diseases and stroke prevention. elements.quote: Results of our review are in concordance with that of a Cochrane review by Uthman et al in 2015 which assessed the effects of multiple risk factors intervention for primary prevention of CVDs.[14] Ebrahim in 2011 had also demonstrated similar results.[52] However both these reviews did not focus on the role of CHW as a change agent. elements.reason: The discussion explicitly compares the review's findings with prior reviews and other evidence (Cochrane review, Ebrahim 2011, and recent reviews), placing the results in the context of existing literature and noting similarities and differences in focus and quality.

elements.quote: A major limitation observed was the low magnitude of effect and quality of evidence in study trials included in this review. A probable reason could have been the nature of studies (community based studies, as against controlled clinical settings) which dilutes the effect of interventions due to within subject and within cluster differences. Implementation of interventions by less trained staff could also have contributed to a decrease in effect size. Most of the trials reported training the health workers in a workshop or a short course, which could also have affected the performance. With the exception of a trial by Jafar et al, all other included trials relied on short-term effects of interventions and failed to report issues related to behaviour relapse, as in interventions targeting medication adherence, weight loss or smoking. Also, shorter length of follow ups fail to capture 'saturation effects' of primary prevention interventions implemented at population level.[53] ... The differences in study settings, baseline differences, differences in follow up periods or differences in intervention content and delivery methods led to considerable PLOS heterogeneity in evidence. We tried to address this by use of a 'maximum 75% heterogeneity cut-off criteria' for selection of results of risk factors for pooling. The review has also left several questions unanswered, primarily due to paucity of trials, especially in the field of cancer, COPD and stroke. This gap in information needs to be filled, which requires further research using robust trial designs and longer follow-up periods. More good quality trials need to be designed and implemented to study the effects of interventions. Measurement approaches should be made more objective and reliance on self-reported parameters should be reduced in order to enhance methodological robustness of the trials.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly describes multiple limitations of the included evidence—low effect sizes and low quality, community-based study designs diluting effects, limited training of implementers, short follow-ups, heterogeneity across studies, paucity of trials for some conditions, and measurement/ self-report issues—thereby addressing limitations of the evidence included in the review.

elements.quote: Minor and major methodological challenges in synthesising the evidence should also be understood while interpreting the results of this review. As we combined the results of individual and cluster randomised controlled trials, suitable analytical methods were used to make the trial results comparable. Second, the settings in which the trials were conducted varied despite developing country settings. The type of CHW, nature of interventions also were not exactly similar. The differences in study settings, baseline differences, differences in follow up periods or differences in intervention content and delivery methods led to considerable ... heterogeneity in evidence.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly notes limitations of the review's synthesis process (combining individual and cluster RCTs), heterogeneity due to varied settings/interventions, and methodological challenges in synthesising the evidence.

elements.quote: The differences in study settings, baseline differences, differences in follow up periods or differences in intervention content and delivery methods led to considerable ... heterogeneity in evidence. elements.quote: The evidence suggests that the CHWs may be effective in altering the risk factors for NCDs for people in developing countries. While community health workers' led interventions were not very successful in altering individuals' behaviour patterns, modifications in physical parameters, such as systolic and diastolic blood pressure was clearly observed. Community health workers were also able to introduce and sustain a long term control on HbA1C levels among diabetics, however short term effects observed were not statistically significant. It was also observed that while CHW led interventions were able to significantly reduce cholesterol levels among participants, self-efficacy and medication adherence still remain a cause of concern.
elements.reason: Explicit discussion of how CHW interventions affect clinical and behavioral outcomes, describing where they are effective (blood pressure, HbA1C, cholesterol) and where they are less successful (behaviour change, self-efficacy), which informs practical implications for implementation.

elements.quote: As countries turn towards universal healthcare coverage, policymakers will need high quality evidence about efficient strategies for NCDs, particularly those focusing on prevention, to avoid burdening health systems with large numbers of individuals with chronic conditions that are expensive to treat. ... So, in this sense, a process of task shifting will be required in order to extend services to those who need them in the face of a shortage of physicians, nurses, and other higher-level health professionals. This review fulfils a palpable deficiency in terms of evidence of CHW effectiveness from low and middle income countries.
elements.reason: Direct statements addressing policymakers, resource allocation, and task-shifting indicate policy implications and recommendations for health system strategies.

elements.quote: The review has also left several questions unanswered, primarily due to paucity of trials, especially in the field of cancer, COPD and stroke. elements.quote: A major limitation observed was the low magnitude of effect and quality of evidence in study trials included in this review. A probable reason could have been the nature of studies (community based studies, as against controlled clinical settings) which dilutes the effect of interventions due to within subject and within cluster differences. Implementation of interventions by less trained staff could also have contributed to a decrease in effect size. With the exception of a trial by Jafar et al, all other included trials relied on short-term effects of interventions and failed to report issues related to behaviour relapse, as in interventions targeting medication adherence, weight loss or smoking. Also, shorter length of follow ups fail to capture 'saturation effects' of primary prevention interventions implemented at population level.[53] However, we found that on overall synthesis of results mean follow up for most of the outcomes was more than 12 months, which adds strength to the evidence. Minor and major methodological challenges in synthesising the evidence should also be understood while interpreting the results of this review.
elements.reason: The Discussion section explicitly identifies limitations of the included studies/evidence, including low effect size and low quality of evidence, probable reasons (study nature, implementation by less trained staff), short-term effects and missing relapse outcomes, insufficient follow-up to capture saturation effects, and methodological challenges affecting interpretation.
The Discussion describes limitations of the included studies and heterogeneity (e.g., short follow-up, trial effects), but it does not explicitly discuss limitations of the review processes used.
No review-process limitation is explicitly stated; therefore, the potential impact of each review-process limitation on the results is not discussed.

elements.quote: As countries turn towards universal healthcare coverage, policymakers will need high quality evidence about efficient strategies for NCDs, particularly those focusing on prevention, to avoid burdening health systems with large numbers of individuals with chronic conditions that are expensive to treat.

elements.quote: The review has also left several questions unanswered, primarily due to paucity of trials, especially in the field of cancer, COPD and stroke.
